blocks.text: Amino acids are an important group of compounds that contain both a basic amino group (-NH2) and an acidic carboxylic acid group (-COOH). They are therefore amphoteric: they can behave as both acids and bases. The general structure of the alpha-amino acids (2-aminocarboxylic acids) is H2N-CH(R)-COOH.

blocks.alt: Three displayed structures in dashed boxes: the general structure of an amino acid, R-C(H)(NH2)-COOH; the natural structure, with the H of COOH circled and a curved arrow taking it to the lone pair of NH2; and the zwitter ionic structure, R-C(H)(NH3+)-COO-.
blocks.caption: The general structure of an amino acid, its natural structure and its zwitter ionic structure (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 129).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed zwitterion shows 'COO' and 'Nh3' without charges; they are COO- and NH3+, as drawn above.

An alpha-amino acid exists as a dipolar ion called a zwitterion, with a positive and a negative end in the same molecule. In forming the zwitterion a proton passes from the carboxyl group to the amino group: H3N+-CH(R)-COO-. The dipolar structure is also called an internal salt.

The R group is the part that varies between amino acids. The simplest amino acid is glycine (aminoethanoic acid), in which R is a hydrogen atom; in alanine (2-aminopropanoic acid) R is a methyl group, -CH3. Except glycine, all alpha-amino acids are chiral. Of the 20 alpha-amino acids, 10 are essential (the body cannot make them) and 10 are non-essential.

blocks.alt: Glycine, H-C(H)(NH2)-COOH, and alanine, CH3-C(H)(NH2)-COOH, drawn displayed.
blocks.caption: Glycine and alanine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 129).
